catalog_quote: [Webb 1974: 50, sec. 2.2.3] Stress, which is related to vowel quality and length, may occur on either the first or second vowel themselves. In no case is their combined phonetic length equal to only one unit of length. [p. 51, sec. 2.2.4] Long vowels have been interpreted as single lengthened vowels of two units length. Stress is always at the onset and only a single pulse is heard. /a/ is regarded as a lengthened /ʌ/ and this fits the distribution pattern. Repetitions of /i/ and /u/ occur with stress on the first vowel and two definite pulses. These are interpreted as a sequence of two vowels. new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Checked against the page images (page render renders of the saved PDFs), not just the scanned. (52-page scan, no text layer): PDF page 6 = printed p. 50, sec. 2.2.3, reads exactly "Stress, which is related to vowel quality and length, may occur on either the first or second vowel them-selves. In no case is their combined phonetic length equal to only one unit of length." (hyphenated across a line break; the scanned file has "then selves", the quote's "themselves" is right). PDF page 7 = p. 51, sec. 2.2.4: "Long vowels have been interpreted as single lengthened vowels of two units length. Stress is always at the onset and only a single pulse is heard. /a/ is regarded as a lengthened /ʌ/ and…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Webb gives no rule for which syllable of a polysyllabic word carries stress. What he states is that stress is tied to vowel quantity and quality: long vowels (/i:/, /a/ [= lengthened /ʌ/], /u:/) are stressed, with the stress at the onset of the long vowel, and the mid vowels e and o also attract stress; in vowel sequences stress may fall on either vowel; word-initial ii/uu sequences carry two stress pulses with stress on the first. Stress is treated as non-contrastive (it is not in the phoneme chart and is not listed among the contrastive features). The reading 'weight-sensitive' is provisional and low-confidence: it captures the stated attraction of stress to long and mid vowels, but the default position in words without such vowels is never stated.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed as such; the 1981 survey remarks that the name Uri is pronounced 'Urii with practically equal stress on both syllables' (p. 10), and 1974 p. 51 describes initial /ii/, /uu/ sequences as having 'two definite pulses'.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. The 1974 paper says intonation was not studied (p. 92); the 1981 supplement adds utterance-level intonation contours and says the exact position of the yes/no-question pitch peak depends on 'the stressed syllable' (p. 7). The 1981 supplement also says the value of mid/central vowels 'in unstressed syllables' was not resolved by the dialect survey (p. 11).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (phonological word; the syllable is 'the unit of stress placement'). Data from citation/elicited forms and a 1,500-word dictionary collected at Siarra village 1965-67; stress marks are not given in the phonemic or phonetic transcriptions, so the statements cannot be checked against the examples.
new_statements.identity_note: Both Webb sources describe the language-level variety urii1240 (no dialect glottocodes exist). Webb 1974 is based on nine months at Siarra (Siara) village with a 19-year-old informant; the 1981 dialect survey (in, p. 10) says Webb lived only at Siara and Fayang, i.e. McElhanon's West Uri, and reports phonemic uniformity across villages with only slight differences in the three eastern (East Uri) villages. Older spelling 'Urii' = Uri.
